China does **not** currently have more retirees than workers.  
Recent demographic data show that the worker‑to‑retiree ratio in China is roughly 3 to 1 (about three working‑age people for every retiree) — the same order of magnitude that the United States has today, though with a slightly higher ratio [PolitiFact](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/may/14/joe-biden/does-china-have-more-retirees-than-workers/).  

The majority of experts agree that this ratio will decline as the population ages, but the change is projected to reach parity (workers and retirees roughly equal) in the early 2050s, depending on how age groups are defined [PolitiFact](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/may/14/joe-biden/does-china-have-more-retirees-than-workers/).  

### Why the ratio is falling

| Factor | Effect on Worker‑to‑Retiree Ratio |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| **Low fertility** – one‑child policy (1980‑2015) and declining birth rates | Fewer young people entering the labor force |
| **Aging population** – China’s median age is rising from <20 in 1971 to ≈43 today and will exceed 60 by 2060 | More people move into the retired age bracket |
| **Early retirement age** – men 60, women 50/55 | Current retirees enter the cohort earlier than in many other countries |
| **Pension system strain** – the national pension fund is projected to become insolvent by 2035 if the ratio continues to fall | Pressure on the system may prompt later retirements and reforms |
| **Economic slowdown** – shrinking labor force and lower wages reduce pension contributions | Less funding for retirees, making the system unsustainable |

These dynamics are documented in several reliable sources:

- **Boris**’ MCP analysis of the aging crisis: the pension fund may run out of money by 2035 [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-china-68595450).  
- **Economist** warns that by 2050 the population over 60 will reach 520 million, more than the U.S. at the same time [Economist](https://www.economist.com/china/2024/04/09/chinas-high-stakes-struggle-to-defy-demographic-disaster).  
- The **NPR** report notes that China’s planned gradual increase in retirement age (men to 63, women 55–58) aims to ease fiscal pressure as the number of retirees grows [NPR](http://www.npr.org/2024/09/13/g-s1-22510/china-retirement-age).  
- **ForeignPolicy** discusses how the National Social Security Fund could be depleted by 2035 due to the shrinking worker‑to‑retiree ratio [ForeignPolicy](https://foreignpolicy.com/2023/06/29/china-pensions-aging-demographics-economy).

### Bottom line

China’s workforce-to-retiree ratio is sloping downward, but the point at which retirees outnumber workers has not yet been reached. The current ratio of about 3 to 1 is expected to fall to 2 to 1 by 2041 and eventually reach close to 1 to 1 around 2052‑2053, depending on age‑group definitions. Until that point, China has more workers than retirees [PolitiFact](https://api.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/may/14/joe-biden/does-china-have-more-retirees-than-workers/).

Congress does **not** prohibit the National Institutes of Health (NIH) from researching the causes of mass shootings.  
The claim that “Congress prohibits the NIH from investigating mass shootings” is a misunderstanding of the *Dickey Amendment* and its subsequent clarifications.

### What the Dickey Amendment actually says
- In 1996, Congress added language to the federal appropriations bill that read:  
  > “None of the funds made available for injury prevention and control at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention may be used to advocate or promote gun control.”  
  This was originally directed at the CDC, but later extended to the NIH in 2011.  
- The amendment does **not** ban research on gun violence; it only bars the use of federal funds for *advocacy* or *promotion* of gun‑control policies.  
- Because the language was vague and politically charged, federal agencies – especially the CDC – interpreted it as a chilling prohibition and largely stopped funding gun‑violence research for more than two decades.

### Congressional clarification
- In March 2018, Congress included a statement in the omnibus spending bill that clarified the amendment’s meaning: the Department of Health and Human Services – and thus the NIH – may conduct research on the causes of gun violence, provided the research does not advocate for specific gun‑control legislation.  
- The clarification was reiterated by the HHS Secretary, who said the CDC (and by extension the NIH) has the authority to study gun‑related violence without fear of violating the amendment.  
- Since fiscal year 2020, the NIH (along with the CDC, the Office of Justice Programs, and other agencies) has awarded **millions of dollars** in grants to study firearm violence, including studies of mass shootings.  

### Current status
- The NIH is actively funding gun‑violence research; the agency has awarded grants on the causes and prevention of mass shootings.  
- No current law or congressional mandate bars the NIH from investigating mass shootings.

**Sources**  
- [PolitiFact – Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is wrong about a ban on NIH research on mass shootings](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/apr/23/robert-f-kennedy-jr/robert-f-kennedy-jr-is-wrong-about-a-ban-on-nih-re/)  
- [NCBI PMC – The Dickey Amendment on Federal Funding for Research on Gun Violence](https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5993413/)

Adolf Heusinger was **not** Adolf Hitler’s chief of staff, nor did he become a chief of staff for NATO after the war.

**During World II**

* Heusinger was a senior operations officer on the German General Staff.  From 1938‑1944 he led the Operations Division of the Army’s General Staff (OKH) and was promoted to lieutenant general in 1943.  
* When General Kurt Zeitzler temporarily resigned in July 1944, Heusinger acted as chief of the Army General Staff for a short period (about two weeks) and was present in the Wolf’s Lair during the July 20 plot.  That brief assignment does **not** equate to the permanent position of “chief of staff” of the Wehrmacht or of Hitler’s overall command 【Snopes.com】【Wiki】.

**After World II**

* Heusinger was taken prisoner by the Allies in May 1945 and later cleared of war‑crimes charges.  
* He entered the post‑war German military (Bundeswehr) and in 1957 was promoted to full general and appointed **Inspector General of the West German Armed Forces** (the office equivalent to the commander‑in‑chief of the army).  He served in that role until 1961 【Wiki】.  
* In April 1961 he was appointed **Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee**, the senior military advisory body of the alliance.  He served in that position until 1964 【Wiki】.

|--------|---------------|-------|
| 1940‑1944 | Operations Chief (OKH) | Senior staff officer, never the overall chief of staff. |
| Jul‑1944 | Acting Chief of Army General Staff (OKH) | Temporary, two‑week tenure. |
| 1957‑1961 | Inspector General of the West German Armed Forces | Highest-ranked German army officer. |
| 1961‑1964 | Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee | Senior NATO advisory role, **not** the “chief of staff.” |

The claim that Heusinger was Hitler’s chief of staff and then NATO’s chief of staff is therefore incorrect. His wartime role was a senior staff position, and his postwar roles were high‑ranking but distinct from a chief‑of‑staff position.

   * Preserve evidence that could relate to possible violations of the Convention.
